epic_title: Commands, ribbon, menus and startup behaviour
summary: This epic owns every way to reach a periodic note without opening the calendar view first: the command palette, the ribbon icon and its context menu, and automatic note-opening at vault startup. It also owns the calendar view's own entry point (opening and auto-revealing it) and reveal-in-calendar shortcuts. It does not own what a note operation actually does when triggered (NOTE), the calendar view's own grid and interactions once open (CAL), or which granularities are enabled and which note is configured to open at startup (SET) - it only owns how the command surface reacts to those choices.

stories.title: Open the calendar view from the command palette
stories.story: As a vault user who does not want to click a ribbon icon, I want a command that opens the calendar view, so that I can reach it entirely from the keyboard.
stories.rationale: The calendar view has no ribbon icon of its own in the merged design, so the palette command is its only guaranteed entry point.

acceptance_criteria.given: no calendar view leaf is open anywhere in the workspace
acceptance_criteria.when: the user runs the "Open calendar" command
then: a calendar leaf is created in the workspace
the calendar leaf becomes visible and gains focus
acceptance_criteria.evidence: vitest: src/ui/calendarCommand.test.ts > creates a calendar leaf, reveals it and focuses it when none is open / > creates the command leaf active, because the user asked for it; src/adapters/obsidianCalendarLeafAdapter.test.ts > walks create, find, reveal and focus as one sequence / > asks for keyboard focus explicitly, because revealLeaf does not / > creates the leaf active when the caller asked for focus. Creation and the explicit focus request are proven headless against a fake that models dock and visibility state. The clause that focus actually LANDS is testable_by integration and unverified: it needs a live Obsidian host, which this environment has none of.

acceptance_criteria.given: a calendar view leaf is already open
acceptance_criteria.when: the user opens the command palette
then: the "Open calendar" command is not listed
acceptance_criteria.evidence: vitest: src/ui/calendarCommand.test.ts > is listed when no calendar leaf is open / > is not listed while a calendar leaf is visible / > is listed when the leaf exists but is not on screen / > opens nothing while the palette is only checking. Note the reading this settles, agreed with Anna in the implementing pane: "already open" means VISIBLE, not merely existing, because initLeaf parks a leaf in the sidebar at startup -- on the exists reading the command would be hidden forever. Obsidian own palette filtering of a checkCallback command is integration-level and unverified here.

acceptance_criteria.given: a calendar view leaf already exists
acceptance_criteria.when: anything in the plugin attempts to open the calendar view again
then: no second calendar leaf is created
the existing leaf is revealed instead
acceptance_criteria.evidence: vitest: src/ui/calendarCommand.test.ts > reveals the existing leaf instead of creating a second one / > creates one leaf when two callers race, because both see no leaf / > reveals once for a race, rather than once per caller / > makes one leaf when startup and the command race / > opens again after the first open has settled / > does not wedge after a failed open; plus src/adapters/obsidianCalendarLeafAdapter.test.ts > finds nothing when a right-sidebar leaf exists but carries no calendar view. Settled headless, including the concurrency the review rounds forced -- the first race test could not fail and was rewritten to defer creation until both callers had started.

acceptance_criteria.given: the sidebar holding the calendar leaf is collapsed or hidden
acceptance_criteria.when: the user runs the "Open calendar" command
then: the sidebar expands
the calendar view becomes visible
acceptance_criteria.evidence: vitest: src/adapters/obsidianCalendarLeafAdapter.test.ts > is false when the leaf sits in a collapsed right sidebar / > is false when the leaf sits in a collapsed left sidebar / > is false when an ancestor hides the leaf, such as an inactive dock tab / > is true when the leaf sits in an expanded sidebar; src/ui/calendarCommand.test.ts > reveals a leaf hidden in a collapsed sidebar. The decision to reveal is proven; the sidebar actually expanding is Obsidian own revealLeaf behaviour (documented in obsidian.d.ts as uncollapsing a sidebar) and is testable_by integration -- unverified without a live host.

acceptance_criteria.given: the calendar view leaf fails to initialize when the plugin attempts to create it
acceptance_criteria.when: the user runs the "Open calendar" command
then: a notice tells the user the calendar view could not be opened
no partially-initialized calendar leaf is left in the workspace
acceptance_criteria.evidence: vitest: src/ui/calendarCommand.test.ts > notices the failure and leaves no leaf behind when creation fails / > detaches the leaf it just created when revealing it fails / > keeps a pre-existing leaf when revealing it fails; src/adapters/obsidianCalendarLeafAdapter.test.ts > detaches only its own leaf, and the detached one stops being found / > throws when the workspace offers no right sidebar leaf / > detaches the half-built leaf when the view fails to initialize. Rollback ownership is proven headless -- it detaches only the leaf this invocation created, never a pre-existing one. The Notice reaching the user is integration-level and unverified.

stories.rationale: This turns the calendar into a default part of the workspace layout instead of an opt-in view.

stories.title: Reveal the active note in the calendar
stories.story: As someone jumping between many periodic notes, I want a command that jumps the calendar to whatever note I currently have open, so that I can see it in context without manually paging through months.
stories.rationale: Without this, switching notes and switching the calendar's displayed period are two disconnected actions.

decisions.title: A command that cannot act says so
decisions.decision: Running a command whose precondition is not met shows a brief notice naming what was missing. It never fails silently.
decisions.rationale: A command that does nothing and says nothing is indistinguishable from a broken plugin. The old behaviour taught users to stop trusting the command.

stories.title: Avoid a duplicate weekly-note command
stories.story: As someone who wants exactly one command that opens today's weekly note, I want the generated per-granularity week command to be the only one that does this, so that the command palette never offers two entries that do the same thing.
stories.rationale: Two commands opening the same note is confusing and leaves one of them as dead code the moment the generated command set covers week.

decisions.title: Retire the standalone weekly-note command
decisions.decision: There is no separate 'Open Weekly Note' command. The generated per-granularity command set covers it, as it covers every other granularity.
decisions.rationale: It existed because weekly notes predated the generated command set. Keeping both means two command-palette entries doing the same thing, and one of them special-cased in the code.

stories.title: Generate a fixed set of commands for every active granularity
stories.story: As someone who enables a new note granularity, I want the full set of navigation commands to appear for it automatically, so that every granularity gets the same keyboard support without anyone writing new code for it.
stories.rationale: A single template driving all granularities is what keeps the command set consistent and keeps ids stable as granularities are added.

decisions.title: The first release supports day, week, month and year; quarter is reserved
decisions.decision: The set of granularities the first release supports is day, week, month and year. Quarter is a reserved value: the type may name it and configuration may round-trip it, but no command is generated for it, no note is created for it, and no view offers it. Anything asking for quarter behaves the same way as any other granularity that is not enabled.
decisions.rationale: ARCH called quarter supported, NOTE used it as the example of an unsupported granularity, ICE-01 deferred it, and CMD still listed it for generated commands and startup opening. An agent reading the backlog could not tell whether quarter paths must work. This vault has quarter disabled, so nothing is lost by reserving it.

stories.story: As someone browsing notes I have already written, I want a command that jumps to the nearest existing note before or after the one I am viewing, so that I can move through my history without accidentally creating empty notes.
stories.rationale: Pure navigation and note creation are different intents, and conflating them would create unwanted files just from browsing.

stories.rationale: A single icon avoids cluttering the ribbon with one item per granularity while still keeping every active granularity reachable.

stories.title: Exactly one note may open automatically at startup
stories.story: As someone who wants their day to start on a specific note, I want at most one periodic note to open automatically when the vault loads, so that I land exactly where I want without sorting through several auto-opened tabs.
stories.rationale: Automatic startup notes only stay useful if the set of them is small and predictable; more than one defeats the purpose.

decisions.title: The startup note is created for whichever granularity is configured
decisions.decision: If the note configured to open at startup does not exist, it is created, for every granularity that can be configured to open at startup.
decisions.rationale: One source plugin created it for day and week and silently did nothing for the rest. That is an oversight, not a design: a user who asks for the monthly note at startup means it the same way as the daily one.

decisions.title: The first release supports day, week, month and year; quarter is reserved
decisions.decision: The set of granularities the first release supports is day, week, month and year. Quarter is a reserved value: the type may name it and configuration may round-trip it, but no command is generated for it, no note is created for it, and no view offers it. Anything asking for quarter behaves the same way as any other granularity that is not enabled.
decisions.rationale: ARCH called quarter supported, NOTE used it as the example of an unsupported granularity, ICE-01 deferred it, and CMD still listed it for generated commands and startup opening. An agent reading the backlog could not tell whether quarter paths must work. This vault has quarter disabled, so nothing is lost by reserving it.

stories.title: Jump to a note by typing a date in words
stories.story: As someone who thinks in phrases rather than dates, I want to type 'last monday' or 'next week' and land on that period's note, so that I do not have to work out the calendar date first.
stories.rationale: The natural-language date plugin is installed and enabled in this vault, so this command appears today. Dropping it would remove a working feature.

notes: Moved out of ICE-05. The related-files list that shared this modal stays deferred: this story is the date jump only.
The '+N' related-note count badge shown on each suggestion, and the getPeriodicNotes lookup behind it, are deferred to ICE-05. No criterion in this story promises the badge.
Every build UID assigned to CMD is covered by a story; none is accounted for without a separate story.

Most acceptance criteria in this epic need Obsidian's workspace, command and hotkey APIs to observe (testable_by: integration), because the epic is almost entirely about entry points into the host application rather than pure logic. The exceptions are the two per-command id-stability criteria in US-CMD-05 (snapshot-testable as plain string comparisons) and the startup-exclusivity criterion in US-CMD-09 (a pure settings transform, already unit-tested in one source plugin).

US-CMD-06 and US-CMD-07 are written as separate stories on purpose: 'jump' never creates a note and reports when there is nothing to jump to, while 'open next/previous' always succeeds by creating the note. Their acceptance criteria show this contrast rather than stating it as a cross-command comparison.

Commands that call into note creation or lookup (US-CMD-04, US-CMD-06, US-CMD-07, US-CMD-08, US-CMD-09) treat that creation/lookup as a black box owned by NOTE; this epic's criteria only cover whether the command is offered, and what the user sees at the entry point, not how the note itself is built.
